newsitem.title: KENYA: Protests in Kenya broken up, three people killed.
newsitem.headline: Protests in Kenya broken up, three people killed.

text.p: Kenyan police broke up protests in Nairobi and several towns on Monday, beating demonstrators and firing teargas and rubber bullets. Police said three people were killed.
Monday's were the most violent confrontations between police and demonstrators in the runup to this year's general election.

Police spokesman Assistant Commissioner Peter Kimanthi said a mob tried to storm the prison in Nyahururu, 100 km (60 miles) west of Nairobi, to free prisoners and one man was shot dead by prison authorities.
"Another group stormed the Cooperative Bank in the town and a man was shot dead by police," he added. "A policeman was also shot and wounded in Nyahururu by someone shooting from the crowd."

Kimanthi said a boy was earlier killed in the town of Thika in an area where police were not active. He said police were investigating to find how he had died but journalists said they had reports he was shot dead and two other people were wounded.
Riot and paramilitary police fired teargas and rubber bullets to break up rallies in Nairobi. Scores of protesters were severely beaten, some even after they had surrendered.
The demonstrations were called by opposition-backed groups demanding constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections this year and closed down the capital and other areas.
"Moi must go. Moi must go," hundreds of opposition supporters chanted as they marched into the business centre of Nairobi after dozens of police dispersed them from Uhuru Park.
Protesters stoned buses and cars on main highways in the city centre, running down streets pursued by groups of police and members of the paramilitary General Service Unit (GSU).
Police fired teargas and rubber bullets to disperse clusters of protesters outside Nairobi's Serena hotel and beat protesters they caught, kicking and hitting them to the ground.

GSU and police fired teargas inside All Saint's Cathedral and beat several demonstrators including Muturi Kigano, chairman of the unregistered Safina party, and opposition members of parliament Kamau Icharia and Njoka Mutani, witnesses said.

"We were in the middle of the service when they broke in, fired teargas into the house of God. This is Kenyan justice for you. Even in God's house they beat innocent protesters," said the Rev. Peter Njoka.

The Rev. Timothy Njoya, the moderator of the Presbyterian Church of East Africa and an organiser of the demonstrations, was later severely beaten near the cathedral by police wielding wooden pick-axe handles. His assistant was also bady hurt.
Except for the violent game of "cat and mouse" between youths and security forces, the centre of the city was deserted with all shops closed and many barricaded against looters.
The town of Nakuru, northwest of Nairobi, was also closed down as members of Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union, wielding clubs, broke up demonstrations by hundreds of people.
Witnesses said at least two people were injured in Nakuru.
"We have made our point," said Kenyan dissident Koigi wa Wamwere in Nakuru. "Our idea was for people to stay home, for people to attend this rally. Our strategy is not for violence."
On the northern outskirts of Nairobi, witnesses said students stopped vehicles and set them and tyres ablaze in the road and pelted passing cars and trucks with stones.
Many people stayed away from work to avoid the expected clashes between riot police and demonstrators in the city. Most schools were closed and asked parents to keep children at home.

Opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies called for rallies at some 50 sites across Kenya for July 7, a day in Kiswahili known as "Saba Saba" to commemorate a Nairobi rally seven years ago when at least 20 people were killed.
They said supporters would be peaceful unless they were provoked and argued the rallies were not illegal because they are "educational meetings" that do not need police licences.

Despite the campaign, Moi, 73, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for five more years because of electoral rules and splits in the opposition. No date has been set for this year's general election.
